svg.text: The fault chain, from likely cause to fault. Each link shows its evidence and how sure AIcoach is.

text.tspan: Not measurable directly. Pointed
to by your lead hip: turned 31°
at impact, where about 45° is
typical.
Measured: 7% of body height from
address to impact. Key frames:
address and impact.
Verified by the rule table. Your
7% is above the 4% threshold.
It may feel like you stay
down, but at impact your
hips have moved toward the
ball.
Early extension means your hips move toward the
ball on the way down instead of turning. In this
swing they moved 7% of your body height between
address and impact, well past the 4% where AIcoach
calls it a fault. When the hips crowd the ball your
arms lose room, and the hands have to save the
strike. That is a common source of thin and blocked
shots.
The likely cause is hip rotation. Your lead hip had
turned 31° at impact, where about 45° is typical.
When the hip cannot turn further, the body makes
room by pushing forward. So you get two things: the
wall drill to feel your backside stay back, and the
90/90 exercise to give the hip more turn to use.

svg.text: One drill for the fault, one mobility exercise for its likely cause.
Plate 3. Wall drill, seen down the line
Plate 4. 90/90 hip rotation, seen from above

text.tspan: Set up with your backside touching a wall, or your
golf bag. Make slow half swings and keep your
trail glute on the wall through impact.

svg.text: Trains B: it keeps the hips from moving toward the ball.

text.tspan: Sit with both knees bent at 90°, one leg in front,
one to the side. Keep your chest tall and turn
your pelvis from the front shin toward the back
knee.

svg.text: Works on A: more hip rotation to turn into.
See a physiotherapist if you feel pain.

text.tspan: Posture angle changed 6°. Possible from 5°, a fault
from 9°. A possible fault gets no drill or
exercise.
Confidence stays at medium at most while over the
top is measured from the hand path.

svg.text: Keep this swing to compare later
Saving stores the swing clip on the AIcoach server until you delete it.
Answers are based only on this analysis.
No new faults, numbers or drills.

text.tspan: I have read this analysis of your swing.
Ask me about anything in it.
Why does it feel like I’m
staying down when I’m not?
Your head and shoulders stay fairly level,
so the top of your body feels down. The
change happens lower. Between address and
impact your hips moved toward the ball by
7% of your body height.

svg.text: Showing B on Plate 1: pelvis at impact

text.tspan: On the impact frame your backside has come
off the address line. The wall drill trains
exactly that: keep your trail glute on the
wall through impact.
What does “likely cause” mean?
It is the most probable reason for the
fault, but the video cannot measure it
directly. Here it is pointed to by your
lead hip, turned 31° at impact where about
45° is typical. That is why it carries
medium confidence.

svg.text: Show A on Plate 2: lead hip
How do I know the drill is working?
Can I do this drill in a net?
The coach can point at the plates. It cannot
see anything that is not in this analysis.
